segments.text: Last year, attackers slipped malware into npm and PyPI thousands of times. They didn't break in. They published. A stolen token becomes a new version of a package you already trust, and it runs on every machine that installs it.
This is Scout. At US airports, the Beagle Brigade sniffs luggage for what shouldn't cross the border. Scout does that job for package registries.

Every new release on npm and PyPI is pulled within seconds and unpacked in a sandbox, never executed. Semgrep dataflow rules then ask: does a credential file reach the network, or a downloaded payload reach eval, at install time?

Single rules are weak evidence. Thousands of honest packages compile native code at install time. What almost never happens honestly is install-time execution combined with credential theft. Combinations convict.
Every package in this feed is a real release, published today. Scout hasn't barked at a single one.
So here's what a bark looks like, on one of our inert test fixtures: a package called e-x-p-r-e-s, one letter away from express, scoring one hundred.

The evidence is the actual code: a postinstall hook that npm runs automatically, a private SSH key read from the home directory, and an HTTPS request carrying it off the machine. Nothing to download, nothing to notice.

Then an agent running on Guild reads that evidence and makes the call an on-call engineer needs: what the code does, step by step, which credentials to rotate, and how confident it is. Shown our false positives, it answers: likely benign.
Everything lands in ClickHouse, in Tokyo. Every scan, every finding, and nine and a half million real npm registry events, aggregated in under a second.

The hard part was not crying wolf. Our first rules flagged nearly every honest API client, because sending a token in an authorization header looks just like theft. We split the rules by what actually leaks. Real packages dropped to clean. The malware stayed at one hundred.

Finally, we turned Semgrep on the AI that wrote this repo, with Guardian watching the agent. It caught the agent pasting invisible Trojan Source characters into our own Trojan Source detector, then doing it twice more while writing up the fix, because its edits pass through JSON, which decodes the safe escape back into the invisible character.
Beagle Brigade. Static analysis, real-time analytics, and an agent that acts on what it finds. Good boy, Scout.
